overview.headline: Louisiana Purchase doubled nation and deepened sectional and Native conflicts

keyPoints.point: The United States purchased land west of the Mississippi River from France and expanded westward
keyPoints.quote: signed on April 30, 1803, the United States purchased 828,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi River for $15 million.

keyPoints.point: Negotiators were offered entire territory of Louisiana beyond original authorization and agreed to purchase
keyPoints.quote: when they were offered the entire territory of Louisiana

keyPoints.point: Expansion exposed sectional weaknesses over slavery and required fragile compromises to balance free states and slave states
keyPoints.quote: the desire to maintain a balance between "free states" and "slave states" required a series of fragile compromises

keyPoints.point: Ceded lands populated with American Indians across tribes led to conflict and forced removal to reservations
keyPoints.quote: The land ceded in this agreement (and later expansions) was populated with thousands of American Indians across dozens of tribes.

keyTerms.gloss: Louisiana land transaction that expanded the nation westward
keyTerms.quote: In addition, the Louisiana Purchase ignored the potential impact on Native Americans.

keyTerms.gloss: Treaty portion of the agreement covering cession of territory
keyTerms.quote: is made up of the Treaty of Cession and the two conventions regarding the financial aspects of the transaction.

keyTerms.gloss: Compromise intended to maintain balance between free states and slave states
keyTerms.quote: (notably the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850).

keyTerms.gloss: Native peoples living on ceded lands who faced conflict and removal
keyTerms.quote: leading to conflict with Native Americans.

keyTerms.gloss: President who questioned authority to acquire new territory
keyTerms.quote: President Thomas Jefferson was generally a strict interpreter of the Constitution
